claims.text: The initial high-entropy nanoalloy has a single-phase FCC structure.
Adding a small amount of oxide-forming elements can improve the structural stability of a high-entropy nanoalloy at high temperature.
Adding a small amount of oxide-forming elements can improve the chemical stability of a high-entropy nanoalloy at high temperature.
Aluminum or titanium can serve as the proposed oxide-forming additions.
Adding oxide-forming elements causes a thin oxide layer to form on the nanoalloy surface.
The thin surface oxide layer acts as a barrier against further oxidation.
The thin surface oxide layer inhibits degradation of the alloy.
Relative to an otherwise comparable alloy without oxide-forming additions, the modified alloy will have a lower oxidation rate.
Relative to an otherwise comparable alloy without oxide-forming additions, the modified alloy will have a longer lifetime.
The proposed benefit should hold above 500°C, within a stated boundary of 500–1000°C.
High-temperature oxidation tests comparing alloys with and without oxide-forming additions can assess the hypothesis by measuring oxidation rate and microstructure evolution.
The hypothesis is falsified if the alloy with oxide-forming additions does not exhibit a significantly lower oxidation rate than the alloy without those additions.
